# tokenfuse - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tokenfuse/0.3.0/tokenfuse/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#tokenfuse)TokenFuse

**Runtime cost control & security for AI agents** — a drop-in proxy between
your agent and its LLM/tool providers that enforces per-run budgets, detects
runaway loops, offers a kill-switch, and keeps secrets out of the model’s
context.

This is the project’s **umbrella crate**. TokenFuse runs as a service, not a
library dependency: the gateway ships as the `tokenfuse` binary and as Docker
images on GHCR.

`docker run -p 4100:4100 -e TOKENFUSE_MODE=enforce ghcr.io/taipanbox/tokenfuse`Point your provider client at `http://127.0.0.1:4100` and attach a few
`X-Fuse-*` headers. See the [repository](https://github.com/TAIPANBOX/tokenfuse) for the full documentation, the HA
cluster, the hosted Cloud, and the MCP credential-broker.

# pyo3_log - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/pyo3-log/0.13.4/target-redirect/pyo3_log/

## Expand description

A bridge from Rust to Python logging

The library can be used to install a [logger](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.27/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/log/trait.Log.html) into Rust that will send the messages
over to the Python [logging](https://docs.python.org/3/library/logging.html). This can be
useful when writing a native Python extension module in Rust and it is desirable to log from
the Rust side too.

The library internally depends on the [ pyo3](https://docs.rs/pyo3/0.26.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/pyo3/index.html) crate. This is not exposed through the public
API and it should work from extension modules not using

[directly. It’ll nevertheless still bring the dependency in, so this might be considered if the module doesn’t want to use it.](https://docs.rs/pyo3/0.26.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/pyo3/index.html)

`pyo3`[§](https://docs.rs#simple-usage)Simple usage

Each extension module has its own global variables, therefore the used logger is also independent of other Rust native extensions. Therefore, it is up to each one to set a logger for itself if it wants one.

By using [ init](https://docs.rs/fn.init.html) function from a place that’s run only once (maybe from the top-level module
of the extension), the logger is registered and the log messages (eg.

[) send their messages over to the Python side.](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.27/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/log/macro.info.html)

`info````
use log::info;
use pyo3::prelude::*;
#[pyfunction]
fn log_something() {
    info!("Something!");
}
#[pymodule]
fn my_module(m: Bound<'_, PyModule>) -> PyResult<()> {
    pyo3_log::init();
    m.add_wrapped(wrap_pyfunction!(log_something))?;
    Ok(())
}
```
The following example is how this would be performed with the new declarative inline module syntax introduced in PyO3 0.23 and above.

```
use pyo3::prelude::*;
use log::info;
#[pymodule]
mod my_module{
    use super::*;
   #[pymodule_init]
    fn init(_m: &Bound<'_, PyModule>) -> PyResult<()> {
        pyo3_log::init();
        Ok(())
    }
    #[pyfunction]
    fn log_something() {
        info!("Something!");
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#performance-filtering-and-caching)Performance, Filtering and Caching

Ideally, the logging system would always consult the Python loggers to know which messages should or should not be logged. However, one of the reasons of using Rust instead of Python is performance. Part of that is giving up the GIL in long-running computations to let other threads run at the same time.

Therefore, acquiring the GIL and calling into the Python interpreter on each
[ trace](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.27/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/log/macro.trace.html) message only to figure out it is not to be logged would be prohibitively
slow. There are two techniques employed here.

First, level filters are applied before consulting the Python side. By default, only the
[ Debug](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.27/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/log/enum.Level.html#variant.Debug) level and more severe is considered to be sent over to Python. This can
be overridden using the

[and](https://docs.rs/struct.Logger.html#method.filter)

`filter`[methods.](https://docs.rs/struct.Logger.html#method.filter_target)

`filter_target`Second, the Python loggers and their effective log levels are cached on the Rust side on the first use of the given module. This means that on a disabled level, only the first logging attempt in the given module will acquire GIL while the future ones will short-circuit before ever reaching Python.

This is good for performance, but could lead to the incorrect messages to be logged or not logged in certain situations ‒ if Rust logs before the Python logging system is set up properly or when it is reconfigured at runtime.

For these reasons it is possible to turn caching off on construction of the logger (at the cost
of performance) and to clear the cache manually through the [ ResetHandle](https://docs.rs/struct.ResetHandle.html).

To tune the caching and filtering, the logger needs to be created manually:

```
let handle = Logger::new(py, Caching::LoggersAndLevels)?
    .filter(LevelFilter::Trace)
    .filter_target("my_module::verbose_submodule".to_owned(), LevelFilter::Warn)
    .install()
    .expect("Someone installed a logger before us :-(");
// Some time in the future when logging changes, reset the caches:
handle.reset();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#mapping)Mapping

The logging `target` is mapped into the name of the logger on the Python side, replacing all
`::` occurrences with `.` (both form hierarchy in their respective language).

Log levels are mapped to the same-named ones. The [ Trace](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.27/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/log/enum.Level.html#variant.Trace) doesn’t exist on the
Python side, but is mapped to a level with value 5.

[§](https://docs.rs#interaction-with-python-gil)Interaction with Python GIL

Under the hook, the logging routines call into Python. That means they need to acquire the Global Interpreter Lock of Python.

This has several consequences. One of them is the above mentioned performance considerations.

The other is a risk of deadlocks if threads are used from within the extension code without releasing the GIL.

```
use std::thread;
use log::info;
use pyo3::prelude::*;
#[pyfunction]
fn deadlock() {
    info!("This logs fine");
    let background_thread = thread::spawn(|| {
        info!("This'll deadlock");
    });
    background_thread.join().unwrap();
}
```
The above code will deadlock, because the `info` call in the background thread needs the GIL
that’s held by the deadlock function. One needs to give up the GIL to let the other threads
run, something like this:

```
use std::thread;
use log::info;
use pyo3::prelude::*;
#[pyfunction]
fn dont_deadlock(py: Python<'_>) {
    info!("This logs fine");
    py.detach(|| {
        let background_thread = thread::spawn(|| {
            info!("This'll not deadlock");
        });
        background_thread.join().unwrap();
    });
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Logger](https://docs.rs/struct.Logger.html)
- The `Logger`
- [Reset](https://docs.rs/struct.ResetHandle.html)- Handle
- A handle into a `Logger`

# pyo3_log - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/pyo3-log/0.13.4/pyo3_log/index.html

## Expand description

A bridge from Rust to Python logging

The library can be used to install a [logger](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.27/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/log/trait.Log.html) into Rust that will send the messages
over to the Python [logging](https://docs.python.org/3/library/logging.html). This can be
useful when writing a native Python extension module in Rust and it is desirable to log from
the Rust side too.

The library internally depends on the [ pyo3](https://docs.rs/pyo3/0.26.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/pyo3/index.html) crate. This is not exposed through the public
API and it should work from extension modules not using

[directly. It’ll nevertheless still bring the dependency in, so this might be considered if the module doesn’t want to use it.](https://docs.rs/pyo3/0.26.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/pyo3/index.html)

`pyo3`[§](https://docs.rs#simple-usage)Simple usage

Each extension module has its own global variables, therefore the used logger is also independent of other Rust native extensions. Therefore, it is up to each one to set a logger for itself if it wants one.

By using [ init](https://docs.rs/fn.init.html) function from a place that’s run only once (maybe from the top-level module
of the extension), the logger is registered and the log messages (eg.

[) send their messages over to the Python side.](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.27/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/log/macro.info.html)

`info````
use log::info;
use pyo3::prelude::*;
#[pyfunction]
fn log_something() {
    info!("Something!");
}
#[pymodule]
fn my_module(m: Bound<'_, PyModule>) -> PyResult<()> {
    pyo3_log::init();
    m.add_wrapped(wrap_pyfunction!(log_something))?;
    Ok(())
}
```
The following example is how this would be performed with the new declarative inline module syntax introduced in PyO3 0.23 and above.

```
use pyo3::prelude::*;
use log::info;
#[pymodule]
mod my_module{
    use super::*;
   #[pymodule_init]
    fn init(_m: &Bound<'_, PyModule>) -> PyResult<()> {
        pyo3_log::init();
        Ok(())
    }
    #[pyfunction]
    fn log_something() {
        info!("Something!");
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#performance-filtering-and-caching)Performance, Filtering and Caching

Ideally, the logging system would always consult the Python loggers to know which messages should or should not be logged. However, one of the reasons of using Rust instead of Python is performance. Part of that is giving up the GIL in long-running computations to let other threads run at the same time.

Therefore, acquiring the GIL and calling into the Python interpreter on each
[ trace](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.27/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/log/macro.trace.html) message only to figure out it is not to be logged would be prohibitively
slow. There are two techniques employed here.

First, level filters are applied before consulting the Python side. By default, only the
[ Debug](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.27/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/log/enum.Level.html#variant.Debug) level and more severe is considered to be sent over to Python. This can
be overridden using the

[and](https://docs.rs/struct.Logger.html#method.filter)

`filter`[methods.](https://docs.rs/struct.Logger.html#method.filter_target)

`filter_target`Second, the Python loggers and their effective log levels are cached on the Rust side on the first use of the given module. This means that on a disabled level, only the first logging attempt in the given module will acquire GIL while the future ones will short-circuit before ever reaching Python.

This is good for performance, but could lead to the incorrect messages to be logged or not logged in certain situations ‒ if Rust logs before the Python logging system is set up properly or when it is reconfigured at runtime.

For these reasons it is possible to turn caching off on construction of the logger (at the cost
of performance) and to clear the cache manually through the [ ResetHandle](https://docs.rs/struct.ResetHandle.html).

To tune the caching and filtering, the logger needs to be created manually:

```
let handle = Logger::new(py, Caching::LoggersAndLevels)?
    .filter(LevelFilter::Trace)
    .filter_target("my_module::verbose_submodule".to_owned(), LevelFilter::Warn)
    .install()
    .expect("Someone installed a logger before us :-(");
// Some time in the future when logging changes, reset the caches:
handle.reset();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#mapping)Mapping

The logging `target` is mapped into the name of the logger on the Python side, replacing all
`::` occurrences with `.` (both form hierarchy in their respective language).

Log levels are mapped to the same-named ones. The [ Trace](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.27/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/log/enum.Level.html#variant.Trace) doesn’t exist on the
Python side, but is mapped to a level with value 5.

[§](https://docs.rs#interaction-with-python-gil)Interaction with Python GIL

Under the hook, the logging routines call into Python. That means they need to acquire the Global Interpreter Lock of Python.

This has several consequences. One of them is the above mentioned performance considerations.

The other is a risk of deadlocks if threads are used from within the extension code without releasing the GIL.

```
use std::thread;
use log::info;
use pyo3::prelude::*;
#[pyfunction]
fn deadlock() {
    info!("This logs fine");
    let background_thread = thread::spawn(|| {
        info!("This'll deadlock");
    });
    background_thread.join().unwrap();
}
```
The above code will deadlock, because the `info` call in the background thread needs the GIL
that’s held by the deadlock function. One needs to give up the GIL to let the other threads
run, something like this:

```
use std::thread;
use log::info;
use pyo3::prelude::*;
#[pyfunction]
fn dont_deadlock(py: Python<'_>) {
    info!("This logs fine");
    py.detach(|| {
        let background_thread = thread::spawn(|| {
            info!("This'll not deadlock");
        });
        background_thread.join().unwrap();
    });
}
```

[185](https://docs.rs#185)use std::cmp;
[186](https://docs.rs#186)use std::collections::HashMap;
[187](https://docs.rs#187)use std::sync::Arc;
[188](https://docs.rs#188)
[189](https://docs.rs#189)use arc_swap::ArcSwap;
[190](https://docs.rs#190)use log::{Level, LevelFilter, Log, Metadata, Record, SetLoggerError};
[191](https://docs.rs#191)use pyo3::prelude::*;
[192](https://docs.rs#192)use pyo3::types::PyTuple;
[193](https://docs.rs#193)
[194](https://docs.rs#194)/// A handle into a [`Logger`], able to reset its caches.
[195](https://docs.rs#195)///
[196](https://docs.rs#196)/// This handle can be used to manipulate a [`Logger`] even after it has been installed. It's main
[197](https://docs.rs#197)/// purpose is to reset the internal caches, for example if the logging settings on the Python side
[198](https://docs.rs#198)/// changed.
[199](https://docs.rs#199)#[derive(Clone, Debug)]
[200](https://docs.rs#200)pub struct ResetHandle(Arc<ArcSwap<CacheNode>>);
[201](https://docs.rs#201)
[202](https://docs.rs#202)impl ResetHandle {
[203](https://docs.rs#203)    /// Reset the internal logger caches.
[204](https://docs.rs#204)    ///
[205](https://docs.rs#205)    /// This removes all the cached loggers and levels (if there were any). Future logging calls
[206](https://docs.rs#206)    /// may cache them again, using the current Python logging settings.
[207](https://docs.rs#207)    pub fn reset(&self) {
[208](https://docs.rs#208)        // Overwrite whatever is in the cache directly. This must win in case of any collisions
[209](https://docs.rs#209)        // (the caching uses compare_and_swap to let the reset win).
[210](https://docs.rs#210)        self.0.store(Default::default());
[211](https://docs.rs#211)    }
[212](https://docs.rs#212)}
[213](https://docs.rs#213)
[214](https://docs.rs#214)/// What the [`Logger`] can cache.
[215](https://docs.rs#215)#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)]
[216](https://docs.rs#216)#[non_exhaustive]
[217](https://docs.rs#217)#[derive(Default)]
[218](https://docs.rs#218)pub enum Caching {
[219](https://docs.rs#219)    /// Disables caching.
[220](https://docs.rs#220)    ///
[221](https://docs.rs#221)    /// Every time a log message passes the filters, the code goes to the Python side to check if
[222](https://docs.rs#222)    /// the message shall be logged.
[223](https://docs.rs#223)    Nothing,
[224](https://docs.rs#224)
[225](https://docs.rs#225)    /// Caches the Python `Logger` objects.
[226](https://docs.rs#226)    ///
[227](https://docs.rs#227)    /// The logger objects (which should stay the same during the lifetime of a Python application)
[228](https://docs.rs#228)    /// are cached. However, the log levels are not. This means there's some amount of calling of
[229](https://docs.rs#229)    /// Python code saved during a logging call, but the GIL still needs to be acquired even if the
[230](https://docs.rs#230)    /// message doesn't eventually get output anywhere.
[231](https://docs.rs#231)    Loggers,
[232](https://docs.rs#232)
[233](https://docs.rs#233)    /// Caches both the Python `Logger` and their respective effective log levels.
[234](https://docs.rs#234)    ///
[235](https://docs.rs#235)    /// Therefore, once a `Logger` has been cached, it is possible to decide on the Rust side if a
[236](https://docs.rs#236)    /// message would get logged or not. If the message is not to be logged, no Python code is
[237](https://docs.rs#237)    /// called and the GIL doesn't have to be acquired.
[238](https://docs.rs#238)    #[default]
[239](https://docs.rs#239)    LoggersAndLevels,
[240](https://docs.rs#240)}
[241](https://docs.rs#241)
[242](https://docs.rs#242)#[derive(Debug)]
[243](https://docs.rs#243)struct CacheEntry {
[244](https://docs.rs#244)    filter: LevelFilter,
[245](https://docs.rs#245)    logger: Py<PyAny>,
[246](https://docs.rs#246)}
[247](https://docs.rs#247)
[248](https://docs.rs#248)impl CacheEntry {
[249](https://docs.rs#249)    fn clone_ref(&self, py: Python<'_>) -> Self {
[250](https://docs.rs#250)        CacheEntry {
[251](https://docs.rs#251)            filter: self.filter,
[252](https://docs.rs#252)            logger: self.logger.clone_ref(py),
[253](https://docs.rs#253)        }
[254](https://docs.rs#254)    }
[255](https://docs.rs#255)}
[256](https://docs.rs#256)
[257](https://docs.rs#257)#[derive(Debug, Default)]
[258](https://docs.rs#258)struct CacheNode {
[259](https://docs.rs#259)    local: Option<CacheEntry>,
[260](https://docs.rs#260)    children: HashMap<String, Arc<CacheNode>>,
[261](https://docs.rs#261)}
[262](https://docs.rs#262)
[263](https://docs.rs#263)impl CacheNode {
[264](https://docs.rs#264)    fn store_to_cache_recursive<'a, P>(
[265](https://docs.rs#265)        &self,
[266](https://docs.rs#266)        py: Python<'_>,
[267](https://docs.rs#267)        mut path: P,
[268](https://docs.rs#268)        entry: CacheEntry,
[269](https://docs.rs#269)    ) -> Arc<Self>
[270](https://docs.rs#270)    where
[271](https://docs.rs#271)        P: Iterator<Item = &'a str>,
[272](https://docs.rs#272)    {
[273](https://docs.rs#273)        let mut me = CacheNode {
[274](https://docs.rs#274)            children: self.children.clone(),
[275](https://docs.rs#275)            local: self.local.as_ref().map(|e| e.clone_ref(py)),
[276](https://docs.rs#276)        };
[277](https://docs.rs#277)        match path.next() {
[278](https://docs.rs#278)            Some(segment) => {
[279](https://docs.rs#279)                let child = me.children.entry(segment.to_owned()).or_default();
[280](https://docs.rs#280)                *child = child.store_to_cache_recursive(py, path, entry);
[281](https://docs.rs#281)            }
[282](https://docs.rs#282)            None => me.local = Some(entry),
[283](https://docs.rs#283)        }
[284](https://docs.rs#284)        Arc::new(me)
[285](https://docs.rs#285)    }
[286](https://docs.rs#286)}
[287](https://docs.rs#287)
[288](https://docs.rs#288)/// The `Logger`
[289](https://docs.rs#289)///
[290](https://docs.rs#290)/// The actual `Logger` that can be installed into the Rust side and will send messages over to
[291](https://docs.rs#291)/// Python.
[292](https://docs.rs#292)///
[293](https://docs.rs#293)/// It can be either created directly and then installed, passed to other aggregating log systems,
[294](https://docs.rs#294)/// or the [`init`] or [`try_init`] functions may be used if defaults are good enough.
[295](https://docs.rs#295)#[derive(Debug)]
[296](https://docs.rs#296)pub struct Logger {
[297](https://docs.rs#297)    /// Filter used as a fallback if none of the `filters` match.
[298](https://docs.rs#298)    top_filter: LevelFilter,
[299](https://docs.rs#299)
[300](https://docs.rs#300)    /// Mapping of filters to modules.
[301](https://docs.rs#301)    ///
[302](https://docs.rs#302)    /// The most specific one will be used, falling back to `top_filter` if none matches. Stored as
[303](https://docs.rs#303)    /// full paths, with `::` separaters (eg. before converting them from Rust to Python).
[304](https://docs.rs#304)    filters: HashMap<String, LevelFilter>,
[305](https://docs.rs#305)
[306](https://docs.rs#306)    /// The prefix to prepend to all log targets
[307](https://docs.rs#307)    prefix: Option<String>,
[308](https://docs.rs#308)
[309](https://docs.rs#309)    /// The imported Python `logging` module.
[310](https://docs.rs#310)    logging: Py<PyModule>,
[311](https://docs.rs#311)
[312](https://docs.rs#312)    /// Caching configuration.
[313](https://docs.rs#313)    caching: Caching,
[314](https://docs.rs#314)
[315](https://docs.rs#315)    /// The cache with loggers and level filters.
[316](https://docs.rs#316)    ///
[317](https://docs.rs#317)    /// The nodes form a tree ‒ each one potentially holding a cache entry (or not) and might have
[318](https://docs.rs#318)    /// some children.
[319](https://docs.rs#319)    ///
[320](https://docs.rs#320)    /// When updating, the whole path from the root is cloned in a copy-on-write manner and the Arc
[321](https://docs.rs#321)    /// here is switched. In case of collisions (eg. someone already replaced the root since
[322](https://docs.rs#322)    /// starting the update), the update is just thrown away.
[323](https://docs.rs#323)    cache: Arc<ArcSwap<CacheNode>>,
[324](https://docs.rs#324)}
[325](https://docs.rs#325)
[326](https://docs.rs#326)impl Logger {
[327](https://docs.rs#327)    /// Creates a new logger.
[328](https://docs.rs#328)    ///
[329](https://docs.rs#329)    /// It defaults to having a filter for [`Debug`][LevelFilter::Debug].
[330](https://docs.rs#330)    pub fn new(py: Python<'_>, caching: Caching) -> PyResult<Self> {
[331](https://docs.rs#331)        let logging = py.import("logging")?;
[332](https://docs.rs#332)        Ok(Self {
[333](https://docs.rs#333)            top_filter: LevelFilter::Debug,
[334](https://docs.rs#334)            filters: HashMap::new(),
[335](https://docs.rs#335)            prefix: None,
[336](https://docs.rs#336)            logging: logging.into(),
[337](https://docs.rs#337)            caching,
[338](https://docs.rs#338)            cache: Default::default(),
[339](https://docs.rs#339)        })
[340](https://docs.rs#340)    }
[341](https://docs.rs#341)
[342](https://docs.rs#342)    /// Installs this logger as the global one.
[343](https://docs.rs#343)    ///
[344](https://docs.rs#344)    /// When installing, it also sets the corresponding [maximum level][log::set_max_level],
[345](https://docs.rs#345)    /// constructed using the filters in this logger.
[346](https://docs.rs#346)    pub fn install(self) -> Result<ResetHandle, SetLoggerError> {
[347](https://docs.rs#347)        let handle = self.reset_handle();
[348](https://docs.rs#348)        let level = cmp::max(
[349](https://docs.rs#349)            self.top_filter,
[350](https://docs.rs#350)            self.filters
[351](https://docs.rs#351)                .values()
[352](https://docs.rs#352)                .copied()
[353](https://docs.rs#353)                .max()
[354](https://docs.rs#354)                .unwrap_or(LevelFilter::Off),
[355](https://docs.rs#355)        );
[356](https://docs.rs#356)        log::set_boxed_logger(Box::new(self))?;
[357](https://docs.rs#357)        log::set_max_level(level);
[358](https://docs.rs#358)        Ok(handle)
[359](https://docs.rs#359)    }
[360](https://docs.rs#360)
[361](https://docs.rs#361)    /// Provides the reset handle of this logger.
[362](https://docs.rs#362)    ///
[363](https://docs.rs#363)    /// Note that installing the logger also returns a reset handle. This function is available if,
[364](https://docs.rs#364)    /// for example, the logger will be passed to some other logging system that connects multiple
[365](https://docs.rs#365)    /// loggers together.
[366](https://docs.rs#366)    pub fn reset_handle(&self) -> ResetHandle {
[367](https://docs.rs#367)        ResetHandle(Arc::clone(&self.cache))
[368](https://docs.rs#368)    }
[369](https://docs.rs#369)
[370](https://docs.rs#370)    /// Configures the default logging filter.
[371](https://docs.rs#371)    ///
[372](https://docs.rs#372)    /// Log messages will be filtered according a filter. If one provided by a
[373](https://docs.rs#373)    /// [`filter_target`][Logger::filter_target] matches, it takes preference. If none matches,
[374](https://docs.rs#374)    /// this one is used.
[375](https://docs.rs#375)    ///
[376](https://docs.rs#376)    /// The default filter if none set is [`Debug`][LevelFilter::Debug].
[377](https://docs.rs#377)    pub fn filter(mut self, filter: LevelFilter) -> Self {
[378](https://docs.rs#378)        self.top_filter = filter;
[379](https://docs.rs#379)        self
[380](https://docs.rs#380)    }
[381](https://docs.rs#381)
[382](https://docs.rs#382)    /// Sets a filter for a specific target, overriding the default.
[383](https://docs.rs#383)    ///
[384](https://docs.rs#384)    /// This'll match targets with the same name and all the children in the module hierarchy. In
[385](https://docs.rs#385)    /// case multiple match, the most specific one wins.
[386](https://docs.rs#386)    ///
[387](https://docs.rs#387)    /// With this configuration, modules will log in the following levels:
[388](https://docs.rs#388)    ///
[389](https://docs.rs#389)    /// ```rust
[390](https://docs.rs#390)    /// # use log::LevelFilter;
[391](https://docs.rs#391)    /// # use pyo3_log::Logger;
[392](https://docs.rs#392)    ///
[393](https://docs.rs#393)    /// Logger::default()
[394](https://docs.rs#394)    ///     .filter(LevelFilter::Warn)
[395](https://docs.rs#395)    ///     .filter_target("xy".to_owned(), LevelFilter::Debug)
[396](https://docs.rs#396)    ///     .filter_target("xy::aa".to_owned(), LevelFilter::Trace);
[397](https://docs.rs#397)    /// ```
[398](https://docs.rs#398)    ///
[399](https://docs.rs#399)    /// * `whatever` => `Warn`
[400](https://docs.rs#400)    /// * `xy` => `Debug`
[401](https://docs.rs#401)    /// * `xy::aa` => `Trace`
[402](https://docs.rs#402)    /// * `xy::aabb` => `Debug`
[403](https://docs.rs#403)    pub fn filter_target(mut self, target: String, filter: LevelFilter) -> Self {
[404](https://docs.rs#404)        self.filters.insert(target, filter);
[405](https://docs.rs#405)        self
[406](https://docs.rs#406)    }
[407](https://docs.rs#407)
[408](https://docs.rs#408)    /// Sets a prefix to prepend to log targets before sending log messages to Python.
[409](https://docs.rs#409)    ///
[410](https://docs.rs#410)    /// This allows for Python-side arrangements where logging configurations are only
[411](https://docs.rs#411)    /// attached to logging names other than the root.
[412](https://docs.rs#412)    pub fn set_prefix(mut self, prefix: &str) -> Self {
[413](https://docs.rs#413)        self.prefix = Some(prefix.replace("::", "."));
[414](https://docs.rs#414)        self
[415](https://docs.rs#415)    }
[416](https://docs.rs#416)
[417](https://docs.rs#417)    /// Finds a node in the cache.
[418](https://docs.rs#418)    ///
[419](https://docs.rs#419)    /// The hierarchy separator is `::`.
[420](https://docs.rs#420)    fn lookup(&self, target: &str) -> Option<Arc<CacheNode>> {
[421](https://docs.rs#421)        if self.caching == Caching::Nothing {
[422](https://docs.rs#422)            return None;
[423](https://docs.rs#423)        }
[424](https://docs.rs#424)
[425](https://docs.rs#425)        let root = self.cache.load();
[426](https://docs.rs#426)        let mut node: &Arc<CacheNode> = &root;
[427](https://docs.rs#427)        for segment in target.split("::") {
[428](https://docs.rs#428)            match node.children.get(segment) {
[429](https://docs.rs#429)                Some(sub) => node = sub,
[430](https://docs.rs#430)                None => return None,
[431](https://docs.rs#431)            }
[432](https://docs.rs#432)        }
[433](https://docs.rs#433)
[434](https://docs.rs#434)        Some(Arc::clone(node))
[435](https://docs.rs#435)    }
[436](https://docs.rs#436)
[437](https://docs.rs#437)    /// Logs stuff
[438](https://docs.rs#438)    ///
[439](https://docs.rs#439)    /// Returns a logger to be cached, if any. If it already found a cached logger or if caching is
[440](https://docs.rs#440)    /// turned off, returns None.
[441](https://docs.rs#441)    fn log_inner(
[442](https://docs.rs#442)        &self,
[443](https://docs.rs#443)        py: Python<'_>,
[444](https://docs.rs#444)        record: &Record,
[445](https://docs.rs#445)        cache: &Option<Arc<CacheNode>>,
[446](https://docs.rs#446)    ) -> PyResult<Option<Py<PyAny>>> {
[447](https://docs.rs#447)        let msg = format!("{}", record.args());
[448](https://docs.rs#448)        let log_level = map_level(record.level());
[449](https://docs.rs#449)        let mut target = record.target().replace("::", ".");
[450](https://docs.rs#450)        target = match &self.prefix {
[451](https://docs.rs#451)            Some(prefix) => format!("{}.{}", prefix, target),
[452](https://docs.rs#452)            None => target,
[453](https://docs.rs#453)        };
[454](https://docs.rs#454)        let cached_logger = cache
[455](https://docs.rs#455)            .as_ref()
[456](https://docs.rs#456)            .and_then(|node| node.local.as_ref())
[457](https://docs.rs#457)            .map(|local| &local.logger);
[458](https://docs.rs#458)        let (logger, cached) = match cached_logger {
[459](https://docs.rs#459)            Some(cached) => (cached.bind(py).clone(), true),
[460](https://docs.rs#460)            None => (
[461](https://docs.rs#461)                self.logging
[462](https://docs.rs#462)                    .bind(py)
[463](https://docs.rs#463)                    .getattr("getLogger")?
[464](https://docs.rs#464)                    .call1((&target,))?,
[465](https://docs.rs#465)                false,
[466](https://docs.rs#466)            ),
[467](https://docs.rs#467)        };
[468](https://docs.rs#468)        // We need to check for this ourselves. For some reason, the logger.handle does not check
[469](https://docs.rs#469)        // it. And besides, we can save ourselves few python calls if it's turned off.
[470](https://docs.rs#470)        if is_enabled_for(&logger, record.level())? {
[471](https://docs.rs#471)            let none = py.None();
[472](https://docs.rs#472)
[473](https://docs.rs#473)            #[allow(unused_mut)]
[474](https://docs.rs#474)            let mut extra = py.None().into_bound(py);
[475](https://docs.rs#475)
[476](https://docs.rs#476)            #[cfg(feature = "kv")]
[477](https://docs.rs#477)            if record.key_values().count() > 0 {
[478](https://docs.rs#478)                // write structured data to 'extra', serializing the values
[479](https://docs.rs#479)                use log::kv::{Key, Value, VisitSource};
[480](https://docs.rs#480)                use pyo3::types::{PyDict, PyString};
[481](https://docs.rs#481)
[482](https://docs.rs#482)                struct PyDictVisitor<'p> {
[483](https://docs.rs#483)                    dict: Bound<'p, PyDict>,
[484](https://docs.rs#484)                }
[485](https://docs.rs#485)
[486](https://docs.rs#486)                impl<'kvs, 'p> VisitSource<'kvs> for PyDictVisitor<'p> {
[487](https://docs.rs#487)                    fn visit_pair(
[488](https://docs.rs#488)                        &mut self,
[489](https://docs.rs#489)                        key: Key<'kvs>,
[490](https://docs.rs#490)                        value: Value<'kvs>,
[491](https://docs.rs#491)                    ) -> Result<(), log::kv::Error> {
[492](https://docs.rs#492)                        let py_key = PyString::new(self.dict.py(), key.as_str());
[493](https://docs.rs#493)                        let py_value = PyString::new(self.dict.py(), &value.to_string());
[494](https://docs.rs#494)
[495](https://docs.rs#495)                        let _ = self.dict.set_item(py_key, py_value);
[496](https://docs.rs#496)                        Ok(())
[497](https://docs.rs#497)                    }
[498](https://docs.rs#498)                }
[499](https://docs.rs#499)
[500](https://docs.rs#500)                let mut visitor = PyDictVisitor {
[501](https://docs.rs#501)                    dict: PyDict::new(py),
[502](https://docs.rs#502)                };
[503](https://docs.rs#503)                let _ = record.key_values().visit(&mut visitor);
[504](https://docs.rs#504)
[505](https://docs.rs#505)                extra = visitor.dict.into_any();
[506](https://docs.rs#506)            }
[507](https://docs.rs#507)
[508](https://docs.rs#508)            let record = logger.call_method1(
[509](https://docs.rs#509)                "makeRecord",
[510](https://docs.rs#510)                (
[511](https://docs.rs#511)                    target,
[512](https://docs.rs#512)                    log_level,
[513](https://docs.rs#513)                    record.file(),
[514](https://docs.rs#514)                    record.line().unwrap_or_default(),
[515](https://docs.rs#515)                    msg,
[516](https://docs.rs#516)                    PyTuple::empty(py), // args
[517](https://docs.rs#517)                    &none,              // exc_info
[518](https://docs.rs#518)                    &none,              // func
[519](https://docs.rs#519)                    extra,              // extra
[520](https://docs.rs#520)                ),
[521](https://docs.rs#521)            )?;
[522](https://docs.rs#522)
[523](https://docs.rs#523)            logger.call_method1("handle", (record,))?;
[524](https://docs.rs#524)        }
[525](https://docs.rs#525)
[526](https://docs.rs#526)        let cache_logger = if !cached && self.caching != Caching::Nothing {
[527](https://docs.rs#527)            Some(logger.into())
[528](https://docs.rs#528)        } else {
[529](https://docs.rs#529)            None
[530](https://docs.rs#530)        };
[531](https://docs.rs#531)
[532](https://docs.rs#532)        Ok(cache_logger)
[533](https://docs.rs#533)    }
[534](https://docs.rs#534)
[535](https://docs.rs#535)    fn filter_for(&self, target: &str) -> LevelFilter {
[536](https://docs.rs#536)        let mut start = 0;
[537](https://docs.rs#537)        let mut filter = self.top_filter;
[538](https://docs.rs#538)        while let Some(end) = target[start..].find("::") {
[539](https://docs.rs#539)            if let Some(f) = self.filters.get(&target[..start + end]) {
[540](https://docs.rs#540)                filter = *f;
[541](https://docs.rs#541)            }
[542](https://docs.rs#542)            start += end + 2;
[543](https://docs.rs#543)        }
[544](https://docs.rs#544)        if let Some(f) = self.filters.get(target) {
[545](https://docs.rs#545)            filter = *f;
[546](https://docs.rs#546)        }
[547](https://docs.rs#547)
[548](https://docs.rs#548)        filter
[549](https://docs.rs#549)    }
[550](https://docs.rs#550)
[551](https://docs.rs#551)    fn enabled_inner(&self, metadata: &Metadata, cache: &Option<Arc<CacheNode>>) -> bool {
[552](https://docs.rs#552)        let cache_filter = cache
[553](https://docs.rs#553)            .as_ref()
[554](https://docs.rs#554)            .and_then(|node| node.local.as_ref())
[555](https://docs.rs#555)            .map(|local| local.filter)
[556](https://docs.rs#556)            .unwrap_or_else(LevelFilter::max);
[557](https://docs.rs#557)
[558](https://docs.rs#558)        metadata.level() <= cache_filter && metadata.level() <= self.filter_for(metadata.target())
[559](https://docs.rs#559)    }
[560](https://docs.rs#560)
[561](https://docs.rs#561)    fn store_to_cache(&self, py: Python<'_>, target: &str, entry: CacheEntry) {
[562](https://docs.rs#562)        let path = target.split("::");
[563](https://docs.rs#563)
[564](https://docs.rs#564)        let orig = self.cache.load();
[565](https://docs.rs#565)        // Construct a new cache structure and insert the new root.
[566](https://docs.rs#566)        let new = orig.store_to_cache_recursive(py, path, entry);
[567](https://docs.rs#567)        // Note: In case of collision, the cache update is lost. This is fine, as we simply lose a
[568](https://docs.rs#568)        // tiny bit of performance and will cache the thing next time.
[569](https://docs.rs#569)        //
[570](https://docs.rs#570)        // We err on the side of losing it here (instead of overwriting), because if the cache is
[571](https://docs.rs#571)        // reset, we don't want to re-insert the old value we have.
[572](https://docs.rs#572)        self.cache.compare_and_swap(orig, new);
[573](https://docs.rs#573)    }
[574](https://docs.rs#574)}
[575](https://docs.rs#575)
[576](https://docs.rs#576)impl Default for Logger {
[577](https://docs.rs#577)    fn default() -> Self {
[578](https://docs.rs#578)        Python::attach(|py| {
[579](https://docs.rs#579)            Self::new(py, Caching::LoggersAndLevels).expect("Failed to initialize python logging")
[580](https://docs.rs#580)        })
[581](https://docs.rs#581)    }
[582](https://docs.rs#582)}
[583](https://docs.rs#583)
[584](https://docs.rs#584)impl Log for Logger {
[585](https://docs.rs#585)    fn enabled(&self, metadata: &Metadata) -> bool {
[586](https://docs.rs#586)        let cache = self.lookup(metadata.target());
[587](https://docs.rs#587)
[588](https://docs.rs#588)        self.enabled_inner(metadata, &cache)
[589](https://docs.rs#589)    }
[590](https://docs.rs#590)
[591](https://docs.rs#591)    fn log(&self, record: &Record) {
[592](https://docs.rs#592)        let cache = self.lookup(record.target());
[593](https://docs.rs#593)
[594](https://docs.rs#594)        if self.enabled_inner(record.metadata(), &cache) {
[595](https://docs.rs#595)            Python::attach(|py| {
[596](https://docs.rs#596)                // If an exception were triggered before this attempt to log,
[597](https://docs.rs#597)                // store it to the side for now and restore it afterwards.
[598](https://docs.rs#598)                let maybe_existing_exception = PyErr::take(py);
[599](https://docs.rs#599)                match self.log_inner(py, record, &cache) {
[600](https://docs.rs#600)                    Ok(Some(logger)) => {
[601](https://docs.rs#601)                        let filter = match self.caching {
[602](https://docs.rs#602)                            Caching::Nothing => unreachable!(),
[603](https://docs.rs#603)                            Caching::Loggers => LevelFilter::max(),
[604](https://docs.rs#604)                            Caching::LoggersAndLevels => extract_max_level(logger.bind(py))
[605](https://docs.rs#605)                                .unwrap_or_else(|e| {
[606](https://docs.rs#606)                                    // See detailed NOTE below
[607](https://docs.rs#607)                                    e.restore(py);
[608](https://docs.rs#608)                                    LevelFilter::max()
[609](https://docs.rs#609)                                }),
[610](https://docs.rs#610)                        };
[611](https://docs.rs#611)
[612](https://docs.rs#612)                        let entry = CacheEntry { filter, logger };
[613](https://docs.rs#613)                        self.store_to_cache(py, record.target(), entry);
[614](https://docs.rs#614)                    }
[615](https://docs.rs#615)                    Ok(None) => (),
[616](https://docs.rs#616)                    Err(e) => {
[617](https://docs.rs#617)                        // NOTE: If an exception was triggered _during_ logging, restore it as current Python exception.
[618](https://docs.rs#618)                        // We have to use PyErr::restore because we cannot return a PyResult from the Log trait's log method.
[619](https://docs.rs#619)                        e.restore(py);
[620](https://docs.rs#620)                    }
[621](https://docs.rs#621)                };
[622](https://docs.rs#622)
[623](https://docs.rs#623)                // If there was a prior exception, restore it now
[624](https://docs.rs#624)                // This ensures that the earliest thrown exception will be the one that's visible to the caller.
[625](https://docs.rs#625)                if let Some(e) = maybe_existing_exception {
[626](https://docs.rs#626)                    e.restore(py);
[627](https://docs.rs#627)                }
[628](https://docs.rs#628)            })
[629](https://docs.rs#629)        }
[630](https://docs.rs#630)    }
[631](https://docs.rs#631)
[632](https://docs.rs#632)    fn flush(&self) {}
[633](https://docs.rs#633)}
[634](https://docs.rs#634)
[635](https://docs.rs#635)fn map_level(level: Level) -> usize {
[636](https://docs.rs#636)    match level {
[637](https://docs.rs#637)        Level::Error => 40,
[638](https://docs.rs#638)        Level::Warn => 30,
[639](https://docs.rs#639)        Level::Info => 20,
[640](https://docs.rs#640)        Level::Debug => 10,
[641](https://docs.rs#641)        Level::Trace => 5,
[642](https://docs.rs#642)    }
[643](https://docs.rs#643)}
[644](https://docs.rs#644)

[646](https://docs.rs#646)    let level = map_level(level);
[647](https://docs.rs#647)    logger.call_method1("isEnabledFor", (level,))?.is_truthy()
[648](https://docs.rs#648)}
[649](https://docs.rs#649)
[650](https://docs.rs#650)fn extract_max_level(logger: &Bound<'_, PyAny>) -> PyResult<LevelFilter> {
[651](https://docs.rs#651)    use Level::*;
[652](https://docs.rs#652)    for l in &[Trace, Debug, Info, Warn, Error] {
[653](https://docs.rs#653)        if is_enabled_for(logger, *l)? {
[654](https://docs.rs#654)            return Ok(l.to_level_filter());
[655](https://docs.rs#655)        }
[656](https://docs.rs#656)    }
[657](https://docs.rs#657)
[658](https://docs.rs#658)    Ok(LevelFilter::Off)
[659](https://docs.rs#659)}

Provides the reset handle of this logger.

Note that installing the logger also returns a reset handle. This function is available if, for example, the logger will be passed to some other logging system that connects multiple loggers together.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/pyo3_log/lib.rs.html#377-380)#### pub fn [filter](https://docs.rs#method.filter)(self, filter: [LevelFilter](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.27/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/log/enum.LevelFilter.html)) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/pyo3_log/lib.rs.html#377-380)

#### pub fn [filter](https://docs.rs#method.filter)(self, filter: [LevelFilter](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.27/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/log/enum.LevelFilter.html)) -> Self

Configures the default logging filter.

Log messages will be filtered according a filter. If one provided by a
[ filter_target](https://docs.rs/struct.Logger.html#method.filter_target) matches, it takes preference. If none matches,
this one is used.

The default filter if none set is [ Debug](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.27/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/log/enum.LevelFilter.html#variant.Debug).

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/pyo3_log/lib.rs.html#403-406)#### pub fn [filter_target](https://docs.rs#method.filter_target)(self, target: [String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html), filter: [LevelFilter](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.27/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/log/enum.LevelFilter.html)) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/pyo3_log/lib.rs.html#403-406)

#### pub fn [filter_target](https://docs.rs#method.filter_target)(self, target: [String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html), filter: [LevelFilter](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.27/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/log/enum.LevelFilter.html)) -> Self

Sets a filter for a specific target, overriding the default.

This’ll match targets with the same name and all the children in the module hierarchy. In case multiple match, the most specific one wins.

With this configuration, modules will log in the following levels:

```
Logger::default()
    .filter(LevelFilter::Warn)
    .filter_target("xy".to_owned(), LevelFilter::Debug)
    .filter_target("xy::aa".to_owned(), LevelFilter::Trace);
```
- `whatever`=>- `Warn`
- `xy`=>- `Debug`
- `xy::aa`=>- `Trace`
- `xy::aabb`=>- `Debug`

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/pyo3_log/lib.rs.html#412-415)#### pub fn [set_prefix](https://docs.rs#method.set_prefix)(self, prefix: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/pyo3_log/lib.rs.html#412-415)

#### pub fn [set_prefix](https://docs.rs#method.set_prefix)(self, prefix: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)) -> Self

Sets a prefix to prepend to log targets before sending log messages to Python.

This allows for Python-side arrangements where logging configurations are only attached to logging names other than the root.

# ResetHandle in pyo3_log - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/pyo3-log/0.13.4/pyo3_log/struct.ResetHandle.html

This handle can be used to manipulate a Logger even after it has been installed. It’s main
purpose is to reset the internal caches, for example if the logging settings on the Python side
changed.

This removes all the cached loggers and levels (if there were any). Future logging calls
may cache them again, using the current Python logging settings.

---

# Caching in pyo3_log - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/pyo3-log/0.13.4/pyo3_log/enum.Caching.html

```
#[non_exhaustive]pub enum Caching {
    Nothing,
    Loggers,
    LoggersAndLevels,
}
```
## Variants (Non-exhaustive)[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

## This enum is marked as non-exhaustive

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Nothing)

### Nothing

Disables caching.

Every time a log message passes the filters, the code goes to the Python side to check if the message shall be logged.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Loggers)

### Loggers

Caches the Python `Logger` objects.

The logger objects (which should stay the same during the lifetime of a Python application) are cached. However, the log levels are not. This means there’s some amount of calling of Python code saved during a logging call, but the GIL still needs to be acquired even if the message doesn’t eventually get output anywhere.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.LoggersAndLevels)

### LoggersAndLevels

Caches both the Python `Logger` and their respective effective log levels.

Therefore, once a `Logger` has been cached, it is possible to decide on the Rust side if a
message would get logged or not. If the message is not to be logged, no Python code is
called and the GIL doesn’t have to be acquired.

# pyo3_log - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/pyo3-log/latest/pyo3_log/

## Expand description

A bridge from Rust to Python logging

The library can be used to install a [logger](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.27/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/log/trait.Log.html) into Rust that will send the messages
over to the Python [logging](https://docs.python.org/3/library/logging.html). This can be
useful when writing a native Python extension module in Rust and it is desirable to log from
the Rust side too.

The library internally depends on the [ pyo3](https://docs.rs/pyo3/0.26.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/pyo3/index.html) crate. This is not exposed through the public
API and it should work from extension modules not using

[directly. It’ll nevertheless still bring the dependency in, so this might be considered if the module doesn’t want to use it.](https://docs.rs/pyo3/0.26.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/pyo3/index.html)

`pyo3`[§](https://docs.rs#simple-usage)Simple usage

Each extension module has its own global variables, therefore the used logger is also independent of other Rust native extensions. Therefore, it is up to each one to set a logger for itself if it wants one.

By using [ init](https://docs.rs/fn.init.html) function from a place that’s run only once (maybe from the top-level module
of the extension), the logger is registered and the log messages (eg.

[) send their messages over to the Python side.](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.27/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/log/macro.info.html)

`info````
use log::info;
use pyo3::prelude::*;
#[pyfunction]
fn log_something() {
    info!("Something!");
}
#[pymodule]
fn my_module(m: Bound<'_, PyModule>) -> PyResult<()> {
    pyo3_log::init();
    m.add_wrapped(wrap_pyfunction!(log_something))?;
    Ok(())
}
```
The following example is how this would be performed with the new declarative inline module syntax introduced in PyO3 0.23 and above.

```
use pyo3::prelude::*;
use log::info;
#[pymodule]
mod my_module{
    use super::*;
   #[pymodule_init]
    fn init(_m: &Bound<'_, PyModule>) -> PyResult<()> {
        pyo3_log::init();
        Ok(())
    }
    #[pyfunction]
    fn log_something() {
        info!("Something!");
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#performance-filtering-and-caching)Performance, Filtering and Caching

Ideally, the logging system would always consult the Python loggers to know which messages should or should not be logged. However, one of the reasons of using Rust instead of Python is performance. Part of that is giving up the GIL in long-running computations to let other threads run at the same time.

Therefore, acquiring the GIL and calling into the Python interpreter on each
[ trace](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.27/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/log/macro.trace.html) message only to figure out it is not to be logged would be prohibitively
slow. There are two techniques employed here.

First, level filters are applied before consulting the Python side. By default, only the
[ Debug](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.27/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/log/enum.Level.html#variant.Debug) level and more severe is considered to be sent over to Python. This can
be overridden using the

[and](https://docs.rs/struct.Logger.html#method.filter)

`filter`[methods.](https://docs.rs/struct.Logger.html#method.filter_target)

`filter_target`Second, the Python loggers and their effective log levels are cached on the Rust side on the first use of the given module. This means that on a disabled level, only the first logging attempt in the given module will acquire GIL while the future ones will short-circuit before ever reaching Python.

This is good for performance, but could lead to the incorrect messages to be logged or not logged in certain situations ‒ if Rust logs before the Python logging system is set up properly or when it is reconfigured at runtime.

For these reasons it is possible to turn caching off on construction of the logger (at the cost
of performance) and to clear the cache manually through the [ ResetHandle](https://docs.rs/struct.ResetHandle.html).

To tune the caching and filtering, the logger needs to be created manually:

```
let handle = Logger::new(py, Caching::LoggersAndLevels)?
    .filter(LevelFilter::Trace)
    .filter_target("my_module::verbose_submodule".to_owned(), LevelFilter::Warn)
    .install()
    .expect("Someone installed a logger before us :-(");
// Some time in the future when logging changes, reset the caches:
handle.reset();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#mapping)Mapping

The logging `target` is mapped into the name of the logger on the Python side, replacing all
`::` occurrences with `.` (both form hierarchy in their respective language).

Log levels are mapped to the same-named ones. The [ Trace](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.27/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/log/enum.Level.html#variant.Trace) doesn’t exist on the
Python side, but is mapped to a level with value 5.

[§](https://docs.rs#interaction-with-python-gil)Interaction with Python GIL

Under the hook, the logging routines call into Python. That means they need to acquire the Global Interpreter Lock of Python.

This has several consequences. One of them is the above mentioned performance considerations.

The other is a risk of deadlocks if threads are used from within the extension code without releasing the GIL.

```
use std::thread;
use log::info;
use pyo3::prelude::*;
#[pyfunction]
fn deadlock() {
    info!("This logs fine");
    let background_thread = thread::spawn(|| {
        info!("This'll deadlock");
    });
    background_thread.join().unwrap();
}
```
The above code will deadlock, because the `info` call in the background thread needs the GIL
that’s held by the deadlock function. One needs to give up the GIL to let the other threads
run, something like this:

```
use std::thread;
use log::info;
use pyo3::prelude::*;
#[pyfunction]
fn dont_deadlock(py: Python<'_>) {
    info!("This logs fine");
    py.detach(|| {
        let background_thread = thread::spawn(|| {
            info!("This'll not deadlock");
        });
        background_thread.join().unwrap();
    });
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Logger](https://docs.rs/struct.Logger.html)
- The `Logger`
- [Reset](https://docs.rs/struct.ResetHandle.html)- Handle
- A handle into a `Logger`

# arc-swap 1.9.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/arc-swap/~1

# ArcSwap

This provides something similar to what `RwLock<Arc<T>>` is or what
`Atomic<Arc<T>>` would be if it existed, optimized for read-mostly write-seldom
scenarios, with consistent performance characteristics.

Read [the documentation](https://docs.rs/arc-swap) before using.

## Rust version policy

The 1. version will build on any edition 2018 capable compiler. This does not include:

- Tests. Tests build and run on recent compilers, mostly because of dependencies.
- Additional feature flags. Most feature flags are guaranteed to build since the version they are introduced. Experimental features are without any guarantees.

# log 0.4.33 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/log/~0.4.21

# log

A Rust library providing a lightweight logging *facade*.

A logging facade provides a single logging API that abstracts over the actual logging implementation. Libraries can use the logging API provided by this crate, and the consumer of those libraries can choose the logging implementation that is most suitable for its use case.

## Minimum supported `rustc`

See the `rust-version` field in `Cargo.toml` for the current minimum Rust toolchain version.

This version is explicitly tested in CI and may be bumped in any release as needed. Maintaining compatibility with older compilers is a priority though, so the bar for bumping the minimum supported version is set very high. Any changes to the supported minimum version will be called out in the release notes.

## Usage

### In libraries

Libraries should link only to the `log` crate, and use the provided macros to
log whatever information will be useful to downstream consumers:

```
[]
 = "0.4"
```
```
use ;
```
### In executables

In order to produce log output, executables have to use a logger implementation compatible with the facade. There are many available implementations to choose from, here are some options:

- Simple minimal loggers:
- Complex configurable frameworks:
- Adaptors for other facilities:
- For WebAssembly binaries:
- For dynamic libraries:
- You may need to construct [an FFI-safe wrapper over](https://github.com/rust-lang/log/issues/421)to initialize in your libraries.`log`

- You may need to construct
- Utilities:

Executables should choose a logger implementation and initialize it early in the runtime of the program. Logger implementations will typically include a function to do this. Any log messages generated before the logger is initialized will be ignored.

The executable itself may use the `log` crate to log as well.

## Structured logging

If you enable the `kv` feature, you can associate structured data with your log records:

```
use ;
```

# syn 2.0.118 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/syn/~2.0.52

# Parser for Rust source code

Syn is a parsing library for parsing a stream of Rust tokens into a syntax tree of Rust source code.

Currently this library is geared toward use in Rust procedural macros, but contains some APIs that may be useful more generally.

-
**Data structures**— Syn provides a complete syntax tree that can represent any valid Rust source code. The syntax tree is rooted at`syn::File``syn::Item``syn::Expr``syn::Type`
-
**Derives**— Of particular interest to derive macros is`syn::DeriveInput`
-
**Parsing**— Parsing in Syn is built around[parser functions](https://docs.rs/syn/2.0/syn/parse/index.html)with the signature`fn(ParseStream) -> Result<T>`. Every syntax tree node defined by Syn is individually parsable and may be used as a building block for custom syntaxes, or you may dream up your own brand new syntax without involving any of our syntax tree types.
-
**Location information**— Every token parsed by Syn is associated with a`Span`that tracks line and column information back to the source of that token. These spans allow a procedural macro to display detailed error messages pointing to all the right places in the user's code. There is an example of this below.
-
**Feature flags**— Functionality is aggressively feature gated so your procedural macros enable only what they need, and do not pay in compile time for all the rest.

## Resources

The best way to learn about procedural macros is by writing some. Consider
working through [this procedural macro workshop](https://github.com/dtolnay/proc-macro-workshop) to get familiar with
the different types of procedural macros. The workshop contains relevant links
into the Syn documentation as you work through each project.

## Example of a derive macro

The canonical derive macro using Syn looks like this. We write an ordinary Rust
function tagged with a `proc_macro_derive` attribute and the name of the trait
we are deriving. Any time that derive appears in the user's code, the Rust
compiler passes their data structure as tokens into our macro. We get to execute
arbitrary Rust code to figure out what to do with those tokens, then hand some
tokens back to the compiler to compile into the user's crate.

```
[]
 = "2.0"
 = "1.0"
[]
 = true
```
```
use TokenStream;
use quote;
use ;
```
The [ heapsize](https://docs.rs/examples/heapsize) example directory shows a complete working implementation of a
derive macro. The example derives a

`HeapSize` trait which computes an estimate
of the amount of heap memory owned by a value.```
```
The derive macro allows users to write `#[derive(HeapSize)]` on data structures
in their program.

```
```
## Spans and error reporting

The token-based procedural macro API provides great control over where the
compiler's error messages are displayed in user code. Consider the error the
user sees if one of their field types does not implement `HeapSize`.

```
```
By tracking span information all the way through the expansion of a procedural
macro as shown in the `heapsize` example, token-based macros in Syn are able to
trigger errors that directly pinpoint the source of the problem.

```
error[E0277]: the trait bound `std::thread::Thread: HeapSize` is not satisfied
 --> src/main.rs:7:5
  |
7 |     bad: std::thread::Thread,
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ the trait `HeapSize` is not implemented for `std::thread::Thread`
```
## Parsing a custom syntax

The [ lazy-static](https://docs.rs/examples/lazy-static) example directory shows the implementation of a

`functionlike!(...)` procedural macro in which the input tokens are parsed using
Syn's parsing API.The example reimplements the popular `lazy_static` crate from crates.io as a
procedural macro.

```
lazy_static!
```
The implementation shows how to trigger custom warnings and error messages on the macro input.

```
warning: come on, pick a more creative name
  --> src/main.rs:10:16
   |
10 |     static ref FOO: String = "lazy_static".to_owned();
   |                ^^^
```
## Testing

When testing macros, we often care not just that the macro can be used
successfully but also that when the macro is provided with invalid input it
produces maximally helpful error messages. Consider using the [ trybuild](https://github.com/dtolnay/trybuild) crate
to write tests for errors that are emitted by your macro or errors detected by
the Rust compiler in the expanded code following misuse of the macro. Such tests
help avoid regressions from later refactors that mistakenly make an error no
longer trigger or be less helpful than it used to be.

## Debugging

When developing a procedural macro it can be helpful to look at what the
generated code looks like. Use `cargo rustc -- -Zunstable-options -Zunpretty=expanded` or the [ cargo expand](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-expand) subcommand.

To show the expanded code for some crate that uses your procedural macro, run
`cargo expand` from that crate. To show the expanded code for one of your own
test cases, run `cargo expand --test the_test_case` where the last argument is
the name of the test file without the `.rs` extension.

This write-up by Brandon W Maister discusses debugging in more detail:
[Debugging Rust's new Custom Derive system](https://quodlibetor.github.io/posts/debugging-rusts-new-custom-derive-system/).

## Optional features

Syn puts a lot of functionality behind optional features in order to optimize compile time for the most common use cases. The following features are available.

- `derive`- *(enabled by default)*— Data structures for representing the possible input to a derive macro, including structs and enums and types.
- `full`
- `parsing`- *(enabled by default)*— Ability to parse input tokens into a syntax tree node of a chosen type.
- `printing`- *(enabled by default)*— Ability to print a syntax tree node as tokens of Rust source code.
- `visit`
- `visit-mut`
- `fold`
- `clone-impls`- *(enabled by default)*— Clone impls for all syntax tree types.
- `extra-traits`
- `proc-macro`- *(enabled by default)*— Runtime dependency on the dynamic library libproc_macro from rustc toolchain.

## Proc macro shim

Syn operates on the token representation provided by the [proc-macro2](https://docs.rs/proc-macro2/1.0/proc_macro2/) crate
from crates.io rather than using the compiler's built in proc-macro crate
directly. This enables code using Syn to execute outside of the context of a
procedural macro, such as in unit tests or build.rs, and we avoid needing
incompatible ecosystems for proc macros vs non-macro use cases.

In general all of your code should be written against proc-macro2 rather than
proc-macro. The one exception is in the signatures of procedural macro entry
points, which are required by the language to use `proc_macro::TokenStream`.

The proc-macro2 crate will automatically detect and use the compiler's data structures when a procedural macro is active.

# pyo3_log - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/pyo3-log

## Expand description

A bridge from Rust to Python logging

The library can be used to install a [logger](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.27/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/log/trait.Log.html) into Rust that will send the messages
over to the Python [logging](https://docs.python.org/3/library/logging.html). This can be
useful when writing a native Python extension module in Rust and it is desirable to log from
the Rust side too.

The library internally depends on the [ pyo3](https://docs.rs/pyo3/0.26.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/pyo3/index.html) crate. This is not exposed through the public
API and it should work from extension modules not using

[directly. It’ll nevertheless still bring the dependency in, so this might be considered if the module doesn’t want to use it.](https://docs.rs/pyo3/0.26.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/pyo3/index.html)

`pyo3`[§](https://docs.rs#simple-usage)Simple usage

Each extension module has its own global variables, therefore the used logger is also independent of other Rust native extensions. Therefore, it is up to each one to set a logger for itself if it wants one.

By using [ init](https://docs.rs/fn.init.html) function from a place that’s run only once (maybe from the top-level module
of the extension), the logger is registered and the log messages (eg.

[) send their messages over to the Python side.](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.27/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/log/macro.info.html)

`info````
use log::info;
use pyo3::prelude::*;
#[pyfunction]
fn log_something() {
    info!("Something!");
}
#[pymodule]
fn my_module(m: Bound<'_, PyModule>) -> PyResult<()> {
    pyo3_log::init();
    m.add_wrapped(wrap_pyfunction!(log_something))?;
    Ok(())
}
```
The following example is how this would be performed with the new declarative inline module syntax introduced in PyO3 0.23 and above.

```
use pyo3::prelude::*;
use log::info;
#[pymodule]
mod my_module{
    use super::*;
   #[pymodule_init]
    fn init(_m: &Bound<'_, PyModule>) -> PyResult<()> {
        pyo3_log::init();
        Ok(())
    }
    #[pyfunction]
    fn log_something() {
        info!("Something!");
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#performance-filtering-and-caching)Performance, Filtering and Caching

Ideally, the logging system would always consult the Python loggers to know which messages should or should not be logged. However, one of the reasons of using Rust instead of Python is performance. Part of that is giving up the GIL in long-running computations to let other threads run at the same time.

Therefore, acquiring the GIL and calling into the Python interpreter on each
[ trace](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.27/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/log/macro.trace.html) message only to figure out it is not to be logged would be prohibitively
slow. There are two techniques employed here.

First, level filters are applied before consulting the Python side. By default, only the
[ Debug](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.27/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/log/enum.Level.html#variant.Debug) level and more severe is considered to be sent over to Python. This can
be overridden using the

[and](https://docs.rs/struct.Logger.html#method.filter)

`filter`[methods.](https://docs.rs/struct.Logger.html#method.filter_target)

`filter_target`Second, the Python loggers and their effective log levels are cached on the Rust side on the first use of the given module. This means that on a disabled level, only the first logging attempt in the given module will acquire GIL while the future ones will short-circuit before ever reaching Python.

This is good for performance, but could lead to the incorrect messages to be logged or not logged in certain situations ‒ if Rust logs before the Python logging system is set up properly or when it is reconfigured at runtime.

For these reasons it is possible to turn caching off on construction of the logger (at the cost
of performance) and to clear the cache manually through the [ ResetHandle](https://docs.rs/struct.ResetHandle.html).

To tune the caching and filtering, the logger needs to be created manually:

```
let handle = Logger::new(py, Caching::LoggersAndLevels)?
    .filter(LevelFilter::Trace)
    .filter_target("my_module::verbose_submodule".to_owned(), LevelFilter::Warn)
    .install()
    .expect("Someone installed a logger before us :-(");
// Some time in the future when logging changes, reset the caches:
handle.reset();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#mapping)Mapping

The logging `target` is mapped into the name of the logger on the Python side, replacing all
`::` occurrences with `.` (both form hierarchy in their respective language).

Log levels are mapped to the same-named ones. The [ Trace](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.27/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/log/enum.Level.html#variant.Trace) doesn’t exist on the
Python side, but is mapped to a level with value 5.

[§](https://docs.rs#interaction-with-python-gil)Interaction with Python GIL

Under the hook, the logging routines call into Python. That means they need to acquire the Global Interpreter Lock of Python.

This has several consequences. One of them is the above mentioned performance considerations.

The other is a risk of deadlocks if threads are used from within the extension code without releasing the GIL.

```
use std::thread;
use log::info;
use pyo3::prelude::*;
#[pyfunction]
fn deadlock() {
    info!("This logs fine");
    let background_thread = thread::spawn(|| {
        info!("This'll deadlock");
    });
    background_thread.join().unwrap();
}
```
The above code will deadlock, because the `info` call in the background thread needs the GIL
that’s held by the deadlock function. One needs to give up the GIL to let the other threads
run, something like this:

```
use std::thread;
use log::info;
use pyo3::prelude::*;
#[pyfunction]
fn dont_deadlock(py: Python<'_>) {
    info!("This logs fine");
    py.detach(|| {
        let background_thread = thread::spawn(|| {
            info!("This'll not deadlock");
        });
        background_thread.join().unwrap();
    });
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Logger](https://docs.rs/struct.Logger.html)
- The `Logger`
- [Reset](https://docs.rs/struct.ResetHandle.html)- Handle
- A handle into a `Logger`

# pyo3-log 0.13.4 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/pyo3-log/latest/source/CHANGELOG.md

#0.13.4*Support for pyo3 0.29 (#77).
#0.13.3*Support for pyo3 0.28 (#75).
#0.13.2*Support for pyo3 0.27 (#72).
#0.13.1*Allow specifying a logger prefix (#70).
* Support the kv feature (#69).
#0.13.0*Switch to pyo3 0.26 (and drop support for older versions, #66).
#0.12.4*Allow pyo3 0.25.
#0.12.3*Declarative example (docs, #59).
#0.12.2*Allow pyo3 0.24.
#0.12.1*Pass-through exceptions (#57)
#0.12.0*Update to pyo3 0.23, drop older version support.
#0.11.0*Update to pyo3 0.22.
*`Logger` no longer implements `Clone`#0.10.0*Update to pyo3 0.21.
#0.9.0*Bump lowest allowed version of pyo3 to 0.15 ‒ this prevents linking multiple
pyo3 versions together.
#0.8.4*Allow pyo3 0.20.
#0.8.3*LogRecord takes tuple as `args`, provide an empty one and not a `None` (#28).
#0.8.2*Allow pyo3 0.19.
#0.8.1*Don't insist on newest version of pyo3 as a dependency, allow older versions
too.
#0.8.0*Update to pyo3 0.18.
#0.7.0*Update to pyo3 0.17.
#0.6.0*Update to pyo3 0.16.
#0.5.0*Update to pyo3 0.15.
#0.4.1*Docs: Point out the need to handle GIL in around threads.
#0.4.0*Upgrade to pyo3 0.14.
#0.3.1*Don't confuse Trace level with NOTSET in python.
#0.3.0*Upgrade to pyo3 0.13.
#0.2.2*Fix of versioning of dependencies.
#0.2.1*Internal dependency update (arc-swap on 1.0).
#0.2.0*Bump version of pyo3 to 0.12.
#0.1.2*Remove confusing/irrelevant copy-pasted part of README.
#0.1.1*Bug: Remove stray println/dbgs from the code.

# arc-swap 1.9.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/arc-swap/1.9.2

# ArcSwap

This provides something similar to what `RwLock<Arc<T>>` is or what
`Atomic<Arc<T>>` would be if it existed, optimized for read-mostly write-seldom
scenarios, with consistent performance characteristics.

Read [the documentation](https://docs.rs/arc-swap) before using.

## Rust version policy

The 1. version will build on any edition 2018 capable compiler. This does not include:

- Tests. Tests build and run on recent compilers, mostly because of dependencies.
- Additional feature flags. Most feature flags are guaranteed to build since the version they are introduced. Experimental features are without any guarantees.

## License

Licensed under either of

- Apache License, Version 2.0, ([LICENSE-APACHE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-APACHE)or[https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0](https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0))
- MIT license ([LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT)or[https://opensource.org/license/mit](https://opensource.org/license/mit))

at your option.

### Contribution

Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted for inclusion in the work by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

# rustversion - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rustversion/^1/

## Expand description

This crate provides macros for conditional compilation according to rustc
compiler version, analogous to [ #[cfg(...)]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/conditional-compilation.html#the-cfg-attribute) and

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/conditional-compilation.html#the-cfg_attr-attribute)

`#[cfg_attr(...)]`[§](https://docs.rs#selectors)Selectors

- `#[rustversion::stable]`
 True on any stable compiler.
- `#[rustversion::stable(1.34)]`
 True on exactly the specified stable compiler.
- `#[rustversion::beta]`
 True on any beta compiler.
- `#[rustversion::nightly]`
 True on any nightly compiler or dev build.
- `#[rustversion::nightly(2025-01-01)]`
 True on exactly one nightly.
- `#[rustversion::since(1.34)]`
 True on that stable release and any later compiler, including beta and nightly.
- `#[rustversion::since(2025-01-01)]`
 True on that nightly and all newer ones.
- `#[rustversion::before(`- *version or date*- `)]`
 Negative of- *#[rustversion::since(...)]*.
- `#[rustversion::not(`- *selector*- `)]`
 Negative of any selector; for example- *#[rustversion::not(nightly)]*.
- `#[rustversion::any(`- *selectors...*- `)]`
 True if any of the comma-separated selectors is true; for example- *#[rustversion::any(stable, beta)]*.
- `#[rustversion::all(`- *selectors...*- `)]`
 True if all of the comma-separated selectors are true; for example- *#[rustversion::all(since(1.31), before(1.34))]*.
- `#[rustversion::attr(`- *selector*- `,`- *attribute*- `)]`
 For conditional inclusion of attributes; analogous to- `cfg_attr`.
- `rustversion::cfg!(`- *selector*- `)`
 An expression form of any of the above attributes; for example- *if rustversion::cfg!(any(stable, beta)) { ... }*.

[§](https://docs.rs#use-cases)Use cases

Providing additional trait impls as types are stabilized in the standard library
without breaking compatibility with older compilers; in this case Pin<P>
stabilized in [Rust 1.33](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2019/02/28/Rust-1.33.0.html#pinning):

```
#[rustversion::since(1.33)]
use std::pin::Pin;
#[rustversion::since(1.33)]
impl<P: MyTrait> MyTrait for Pin<P> {
    /* ... */
}
```
Similar but for language features; the ability to control alignment greater than
1 of packed structs was stabilized in [Rust 1.33](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/master/RELEASES.md#version-1330-2019-02-28).

```
#[rustversion::attr(before(1.33), repr(packed))]
#[rustversion::attr(since(1.33), repr(packed(2)))]
struct Six(i16, i32);
fn main() {
    println!("{}", std::mem::align_of::<Six>());
}
```
Augmenting code with `const` as const impls are stabilized in the standard
library. This use of `const` as an attribute is recognized as a special case
by the rustversion::attr macro.

```
use std::time::Duration;
#[rustversion::attr(since(1.32), const)]
fn duration_as_days(dur: Duration) -> u64 {
    dur.as_secs() / 60 / 60 / 24
}
```
Emitting Cargo cfg directives from a build script. Note that this requires
listing `rustversion` under `[build-dependencies]` in Cargo.toml, not
`[dependencies]`.

```
// build.rs
fn main() {
    if rustversion::cfg!(since(1.36)) {
        println!("cargo:rustc-cfg=no_std");
    }
}
```
```
// src/lib.rs
#![cfg_attr(no_std, no_std)]
#[cfg(no_std)]
extern crate alloc;
```
